questions.explanationText: The event immediately preceding and producing the final outcome is that upper floors received little water. The first event is an earlier, indirect cause.

questions.questionText: Given the chain 'A software bug duplicated invoices → customers received incorrect bills → billing disputes increased', which statement is correct?

options.text: 'billing disputes increased' causes both earlier events.
All three events are independent.
'A software bug duplicated invoices' directly causes 'billing disputes increased'.
'customers received incorrect bills' is both an effect of the first event and a cause of the last.

questions.explanationText: The middle event—customers received incorrect bills—is caused by the first event and in turn causes the final event. It is the intermediate link.

questions.questionText:
Event I: Congestion increased in nearby neighbourhoods.
Event II: A road accident blocked the tunnel.
The known intermediate event is that traffic diverted to surface streets. What is the best relationship?

options.text: Event II indirectly causes Event I through the intermediate event.
Both events cause the intermediate event.
The events are unrelated.
Event I directly causes Event II.

questions.explanationText: Although the effect is listed first, the causal order is A road accident blocked the tunnel → traffic diverted to surface streets → congestion increased in nearby neighbourhoods. Thus Event II indirectly causes Event I.

questions.questionText:
Causal chain: A scholarship was widely advertised → applications increased → the review committee's workload rose.
How does the first event relate to the last?

options.text: It is unrelated to the last event.
Both are separate effects of the middle event.
It is an indirect cause operating through the middle event.
It is the immediate effect of the last event.

questions.explanationText: The chain is A scholarship was widely advertised → applications increased → the review committee's workload rose. The first event contributes to the last through an intermediate step, so the relationship is causal but indirect.

questions.questionText: A sequence of events occurred: A cooling fan failed in a server; then processor temperature rose; finally, the server shut down automatically. Which event is the immediate cause of the final outcome?

options.text: Processor temperature rose.
No event in the sequence.
A cooling fan failed in a server.
The server shut down automatically.

questions.explanationText: The event immediately preceding and producing the final outcome is that processor temperature rose. The first event is an earlier, indirect cause.

questions.questionText: Given the chain 'The local currency weakened → import costs rose → the retailer increased prices of imported electronics', which statement is correct?

options.text: All three events are independent.
'The local currency weakened' directly causes 'the retailer increased prices of imported electronics'.
'import costs rose' is both an effect of the first event and a cause of the last.
'the retailer increased prices of imported electronics' causes both earlier events.

questions.explanationText: The middle event—import costs rose—is caused by the first event and in turn causes the final event. It is the intermediate link.

questions.questionText:
Event I: Households bought more bottled water.
Event II: A leak contaminated the water supply.
The known intermediate event is that the authority issued a boil-water notice. What is the best relationship?

options.text: Event I directly causes Event II.
Both events cause the intermediate event.
Event II indirectly causes Event I through the intermediate event.
The events are unrelated.

questions.explanationText: Although the effect is listed first, the causal order is A leak contaminated the water supply → the authority issued a boil-water notice → households bought more bottled water. Thus Event II indirectly causes Event I.

questions.questionText:
A warehouse's dispatch accuracy fell immediately after labels began printing with truncated addresses.
What is the most likely direct cause of the accuracy decline?

options.text: Customers opening parcels
The truncated address labels
The colour of the warehouse walls
A future inventory audit

questions.explanationText: Incomplete addresses on labels can directly send parcels to wrong destinations; the other events do not explain the immediate decline.

questions.questionText:
A coastal road was closed after waves repeatedly crossed the sea wall.
Which event is the immediate cause of the closure?

options.text: Waves crossing the sea wall
The existence of the road
The reopening announcement
Drivers choosing other routes

questions.explanationText: Water crossing the sea wall created the unsafe condition that directly prompted closure.

questions.questionText:
After a payroll file used outdated account numbers, many salary transfers failed.
Which is the direct cause of the failed transfers?

options.text: Employees checking balances
Printing salary slips
The end of the month
Outdated account numbers in the file

questions.explanationText: The incorrect account details prevented successful routing of transfers.

questions.questionText:
A retailer's weekend sales rose after it sent discount codes to loyalty members.
Which event is the supported cause of the rise?

options.text: Customers receiving receipts
Sending discount codes
Counting sales on Monday
Changing the staff roster next month

questions.explanationText: The targeted discount gave recipients an immediate incentive to purchase.

questions.questionText:
A server stopped unexpectedly because its power supply unit failed.
Identify the cause rather than the effect.

options.text: Users seeing an error page
The failed power supply unit
The incident ticket
The server stopping

questions.explanationText: Power-supply failure produced the shutdown; the other relevant events are downstream effects or records.

questions.questionText:
A bus reached the terminal late because an accident blocked its route.
What caused the late arrival?

options.text: The terminal clock
The late arrival itself
Passengers leaving the bus
The blocked route

questions.explanationText: The accident-related blockage delayed travel and caused the late arrival.

questions.questionText:
Seedlings died after irrigation water did not reach the field for a week.
Which is the best-supported cause?

options.text: Counting the dead seedlings
The price of farm tools
Lack of irrigation water
Harvesting a nearby field

questions.explanationText: The stated prolonged lack of water explains the seedling loss.

questions.questionText:
Customers abandoned checkout when the payment page took more than a minute to load.
Which event is the immediate cause of abandonment?

options.text: The slow payment page
A later support survey
The abandoned carts
The daily sales report

questions.explanationText: The excessive load time directly led customers to leave checkout.

questions.questionText:
A machine produced rough surfaces after its cutting tool became blunt.
Choose the direct cause.

options.text: Inspection of the rough parts
The blunt cutting tool
Packaging of finished parts
The operator's lunch break

questions.explanationText: A blunt tool directly degrades the machined surface finish.

questions.questionText:
A classroom presentation was postponed when the projector would not power on.
What is the immediate cause of postponement?

options.text: Students taking notes
The next class period
The projector failure
The postponement notice

questions.explanationText: The unusable projector prevented the scheduled presentation.

questions.questionText:
A company's cloud bill increased after a test environment was mistakenly left running all month.
Which event caused the higher bill?

options.text: The finance meeting
The continuously running test environment
Deleting an old report
Reviewing the invoice

questions.explanationText: Continuous resource use accumulated charges and caused the bill increase.

questions.questionText:
The number of defective seals rose after the sealing machine's temperature controller drifted out of calibration.
Identify the likely cause.

options.text: The defect count
Customer refunds
Controller miscalibration
A later maintenance report

questions.explanationText: Incorrect temperature control directly produced poor seals.

questions.questionText:
A train was cancelled after floodwater covered a section of track.
Which is the causal event?

options.text: Passengers requesting refunds
Floodwater on the track
The timetable display
The cancellation

questions.explanationText: The unsafe flooded track led the operator to cancel the train.

questions.questionText:
An account was locked after five incorrect passwords were entered.
Which event directly triggered the lock?

options.text: Reading the security policy
A later password reset
The account lock
Five incorrect password entries

questions.explanationText: The configured threshold of failed attempts triggered the lock.

questions.questionText:
A restaurant discarded frozen food after a prolonged power cut thawed it.
What caused the food to be discarded?

options.text: Ordering replacement stock
Writing the disposal record
Thawing during the power cut
Cleaning the freezer

questions.explanationText: The loss of safe frozen storage made disposal necessary.

questions.questionText:
The placement portal extended a test window because its login service was unavailable for two hours.
Which event caused the extension?

options.text: Candidates reading email
The login-service outage
Publishing scores later
The extension announcement

questions.explanationText: The outage prevented access during the original window, prompting the extension.

questions.questionText:
A field's soil eroded rapidly after vegetation was removed from a slope.
Identify the contributing cause stated in the scenario.

options.text: Removal of vegetation
A map of the slope
The lower field boundary
Measurement of soil loss

questions.explanationText: Vegetation normally protects and binds soil; removing it increased erosion.

questions.questionText:
A store placed extra staff at billing counters, and average queue time then fell while customer volume stayed constant.
Which event is the supported cause of the shorter queues?

options.text: Customers joining queues
Measuring waiting time
Adding billing staff
Keeping the store logo unchanged

questions.explanationText: With volume constant, added counter capacity provides the stated mechanism for reduced waiting.

questions.questionText:
A storm broke several transmission lines.
Which option is the most immediate likely effect?

options.text: A power interruption in connected areas
Unrelated office recruitment
The storm being caused by darkness
A decrease in textbook printing

questions.explanationText: Broken transmission lines interrupt electricity delivery to connected areas.

questions.questionText:
A software patch corrected the calculation used for tax totals.
Which is the direct expected effect?

options.text: Internet speed increases everywhere
New invoices calculate tax correctly
The original bug becomes the patch's effect
Office rent decreases

questions.explanationText: Correcting the calculation should directly make subsequent invoice totals accurate.

questions.questionText:
The city added twenty buses to an overcrowded route without changing demand.
What is the most likely immediate effect?

options.text: All private vehicles disappear
Rail fares automatically double
The route causes the buses to be manufactured
More passenger capacity on that route

questions.explanationText: Additional buses directly increase available route capacity; broader outcomes are not guaranteed.

questions.questionText:
A supplier reduced its delivery lead time from ten days to four days.
Which is the direct operational effect for regular orders?

options.text: Orders can arrive sooner
Demand must double
The supplier's founding date changes
The buyer's factory becomes larger

questions.explanationText: A shorter lead time directly permits earlier arrival; it does not guarantee demand or expansion.

questions.questionText:
A company enabled multi-factor authentication for remote access.
Which is the most defensible direct effect?

options.text: Remote login requires an additional verification factor
Network bandwidth doubles
Employees no longer need usernames
All cyberattacks become impossible

questions.explanationText: The control directly adds a verification step; it reduces some risks but does not eliminate every attack.

questions.questionText:
A school shifted the first class from 8:00 to 8:30 a.m.
Which immediate effect follows by policy?

options.text: The school year becomes shorter
The first class begins thirty minutes later
All buses use less fuel
Every student's marks improve

questions.explanationText: The schedule change directly alters class start time; the other outcomes are unsupported.

questions.questionText:
A pump began sending water into an empty tank faster than water was leaving it.
What is the direct effect while this condition continues?

options.text: Rainfall necessarily begins
The tank's capacity changes
The tank's water level rises
The pump is caused by the rising level

questions.explanationText: Net inflow is positive, so stored volume and water level rise.

questions.questionText:
A product's listed price was reduced while all taxes and quantities stayed unchanged.
Which direct effect occurs for one unit?

options.text: Product quality automatically rises
The pre-tax amount paid per unit decreases
Production necessarily stops
Competitors must close

questions.explanationText: With other terms fixed, the reduced listed price lowers the amount paid for the unit.

questions.questionText:
A road authority switched off a malfunctioning traffic signal and deployed police to direct vehicles.
What is the immediate effect of the deployment?

options.text: The original fault repairs itself
Fuel prices fall
Traffic receives manual direction at the junction
The road becomes shorter

questions.explanationText: Police deployment substitutes manual control for the unavailable signal.

questions.questionText:
A database backup completed successfully before a disk failed.
What direct benefit can the backup provide?

options.text: Permanent elimination of downtime
Prevention of every disk failure
A recoverable copy of earlier data
Automatic correction of all software bugs

questions.explanationText: The backup supplies a copy from which data can be restored; it does not prevent hardware failure.

questions.questionText:
The factory replaced a leaking compressed-air hose.
Which direct effect is most likely?

options.text: Other unrelated hoses become new
Production demand increases automatically
Air loss through that leak stops
All factory energy use becomes zero

questions.explanationText: Repairing the hose removes that specific leakage path.

questions.questionText:
A library extended its closing time by two hours.
Which outcome follows directly?

options.text: The building gains another floor
The library is available to users for two additional hours
Every visitor reads two more books
Book prices fall

questions.explanationText: The policy directly increases opening availability; user behaviour is not guaranteed.

questions.questionText:
A firewall rule blocked traffic from a confirmed malicious address.
Which is the immediate effect?

options.text: The attacker repairs the firewall
Connections from that address are denied by the firewall
Every malicious address is eliminated
The internet becomes faster for all users

questions.explanationText: The rule directly denies matching connections, but makes no claim about all threats.

questions.questionText:
A company moved frequently accessed files from tape to solid-state storage.
Which direct effect is reasonably expected?

options.text: The files become legally public
All company decisions improve
Electricity supply becomes unlimited
Those files can be retrieved with lower storage latency

questions.explanationText: Solid-state storage offers faster access than tape for the moved files.

questions.questionText:
A blocked storm-water drain was cleared before forecast rain.
Which direct effect did clearing produce?

options.text: Water can flow through that drain again
All city flooding becomes impossible
The road gradient changes
Rain is guaranteed not to fall

questions.explanationText: Removing the blockage restores the drainage path; it cannot guarantee citywide outcomes.

questions.questionText:
A retailer added a second staffed returns counter.
Assuming the same arrival rate, what immediate capacity effect follows?

options.text: Product defects disappear
More returns can be processed simultaneously
Sales tax changes
No customer will ever wait

questions.explanationText: A second staffed counter directly increases simultaneous service capacity, though queues may still occur.

questions.questionText:
An instructor uploaded recorded lectures for an existing course.
Which direct effect is established?

options.text: Every student earns a higher grade
Enrolled students gain on-demand access to those lectures
Internet outages end
Live classes become unnecessary

questions.explanationText: Uploading recordings creates access; improved grades are possible but not guaranteed.

questions.questionText: A secure door opens only when a valid badge is scanned and the correct PIN is entered. Mira scanned a valid badge but entered the wrong PIN. What follows?

options.text: The information establishes no outcome.
The badge alone is sufficient, so the door opens.
The wrong PIN causes the badge to become valid.
The door remains locked because one required condition failed.

questions.explanationText: Both stated conditions are required. A valid badge is necessary but not sufficient by itself; the wrong PIN prevents opening.

questions.questionText: A machine starts only if the safety guard is closed and the emergency stop is released. The guard is closed, but the emergency stop remains engaged. Which conclusion is causal?

options.text: The closed guard alone starts the machine.
The machine cannot start under the stated control logic.
Starting the machine closes the guard.
Both controls are irrelevant.

questions.explanationText: The start condition is conjunctive: both requirements must hold. One unmet requirement is enough to prevent starting.

questions.questionText: A scholarship is awarded only to applicants who meet the grade cutoff and submit income documents. Ravi meets the cutoff but submits no documents. What is the correct assessment?

options.text: Missing documents improve eligibility.
The award causes document submission.
Meeting the cutoff alone is insufficient for the award.
The cutoff guarantees the award.

questions.explanationText: The scenario explicitly requires both conditions, so the grade cutoff is necessary but not sufficient.

questions.questionText: A server enters maintenance mode whenever either the temperature alarm or the power alarm is active. The temperature alarm activates. Is that sufficient?

options.text: The alarms are unrelated to maintenance mode.
Maintenance mode causes the alarm.
Yes; either alarm alone is sufficient to trigger maintenance mode.
No; both alarms must activate.

questions.explanationText: The rule uses 'either', making each alarm independently sufficient.

questions.questionText: A loan application proceeds to review only when identity verification is complete. Identity verification completed. Does approval necessarily follow?

options.text: Approval causes verification to fail.
The application must be rejected.
Yes. Verification is sufficient for approval.
No. Verification is necessary for review but does not guarantee approval.

questions.explanationText: Completion permits review; other credit and policy checks may still determine approval.

questions.questionText: A candidate can sit the assessment only after registering and receiving an admit card. She registered but has not received the card. Which option is valid?

options.text: Registration alone is insufficient to sit the assessment.
Registration guarantees entry.
Sitting the assessment causes registration.
The admit card is merely an effect of the exam result.

questions.explanationText: Both prerequisites are stated. Without the admit card, the necessary set of conditions is incomplete.

questions.questionText: A fire alarm sounds if any one smoke detector sends a confirmed signal. One detector sends a confirmed signal. What relation holds?

options.text: The alarm is the cause of the detector signal.
No causal outcome can be inferred.
Every detector must signal first.
The signal is sufficient under the stated rule to sound the alarm.

questions.explanationText: The rule requires any one confirmed detector signal, so this event meets a sufficient condition.

questions.questionText: A package is dispatched only after payment clears and stock is allocated. Payment clears, but no stock is available. What follows?

options.text: Dispatch creates stock.
Cleared payment alone guarantees dispatch.
Payment and stock are independent of dispatch.
Dispatch cannot occur yet because allocation is also required.

questions.explanationText: Both conditions are necessary; absence of allocated stock blocks dispatch.

questions.questionText: A backup is restored only if the backup is intact and the decryption key is available. The key is available, but the backup is corrupted. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Corruption improves recoverability.
The key alone guarantees restoration.
The available key is insufficient; restoration cannot complete.
Restoration caused the corruption.

questions.explanationText: An intact backup and key are jointly required. Corruption defeats one necessary condition.

questions.questionText: A student passes a module if the weighted total is at least 50 and laboratory attendance is at least 75%. The total is 62, but attendance is 68%. What is the result under the rule?

options.text: A total above 50 is sufficient by itself.
Attendance is caused by the final result.
The rule guarantees a pass.
The student does not pass because the attendance condition fails.

questions.explanationText: The rule requires both the score and attendance threshold; only one is met.

questions.questionText: A cooling system starts when both the sensor detects overheating and the controller is powered. Overheating is detected, but the controller has no power. Identify the logic.

options.text: Detection alone is not sufficient to start cooling.
Cooling causes the controller to lose power.
The controller state cannot affect cooling.
Detection necessarily starts cooling.

questions.explanationText: The controller power is a second necessary condition, so detection by itself cannot trigger operation.

questions.questionText: An online transfer executes only after sufficient balance, a valid beneficiary, and OTP confirmation are present. The first two conditions hold, but OTP confirmation fails.

options.text: Execution causes OTP failure.
The first two conditions are sufficient.
Beneficiary validity becomes irrelevant to every transfer.
The transfer does not execute because one necessary condition is missing.

questions.explanationText: All three specified conditions are required. Failed OTP confirmation prevents execution.

questions.questionText: A warehouse offers same-day dispatch when an order arrives before noon and all items are in stock. An in-stock order arrives at 11 a.m. Is this sufficient under the stated policy?

options.text: Stock status has no role.
Yes, both stated conditions are met.
No, because an evening arrival is also required.
Dispatch causes the order to arrive earlier.

questions.explanationText: Arrival before noon and stock availability are jointly sufficient under the policy, and both are satisfied.

questions.questionText: A vehicle's engine starts only if the key is authenticated; authentication succeeds. Can we conclude the engine must start?

options.text: No. Authentication is necessary, but other conditions such as battery power may still be required.
Yes. The word 'only' makes authentication sufficient.
Starting authenticates the key after the fact.
Authentication guarantees fuel availability.

questions.explanationText: 'Only if' states a necessary condition, not a complete sufficient set. The engine may still fail for another reason.

questions.questionText: A promotion guarantees free delivery for orders above ₹1,000 placed through the app. An app order totals ₹1,250. What follows?

options.text: No relation can be established.
The stated conditions are sufficient for free delivery under the promotion.
The order must be cancelled.
Free delivery causes the order value to exceed ₹1,000.

questions.explanationText: The order meets both explicit promotional conditions, so free delivery follows.

questions.questionText: High humidity increases the probability of mould when ventilation is poor. A room is humid but well ventilated. What is justified?

options.text: Mould is certain because humidity is present.
Good ventilation causes humidity in every case.
Mould must already have caused the humidity.
Humidity alone does not establish that mould will occur.

questions.explanationText: The statement describes increased probability under combined conditions, not a guarantee from humidity alone.

questions.questionText: Completing more practice tests can improve familiarity with question formats. Arjun completes more tests. Which conclusion is warranted?

options.text: The score causes the practice tests.
His final score must increase.
His familiarity may improve, but a higher score is not guaranteed.
Practice has no possible effect.

questions.explanationText: Practice provides a plausible probabilistic benefit, not a sufficient guarantee of marks.

questions.questionText: A lower price tends to increase demand when other relevant factors remain unchanged. The price falls, but a safety recall occurs simultaneously. What is the best assessment?

options.text: Demand must rise regardless of the recall.
The price reduction alone is insufficient to predict demand because another strong factor changed.
The recall is caused by lower demand.
Price can never influence demand.

questions.explanationText: The usual relationship depends on other factors being stable; the recall breaks that condition.

questions.questionText: An antivirus alert is triggered by either a known malicious signature or suspicious behaviour. A known signature is found. What follows from the rule?

options.text: No alert can occur.
Suspicious behaviour must also be present.
The alert creates the signature.
The signature match is sufficient to trigger an alert.

questions.explanationText: Either listed condition independently triggers the alert.

questions.questionText: For a chemical batch to be released, quality testing must pass. The test passes. Is release guaranteed?

options.text: No. Passing is necessary, but authorization or packaging may also be required.
Release caused the test to pass.
Testing and release are unrelated.
Yes. Every necessary condition is automatically sufficient.

questions.explanationText: The wording identifies a requirement, not the complete set of requirements.

questions.questionText: A login is blocked after three failed attempts within ten minutes. Exactly three failures occur in eight minutes. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The stated condition is sufficient to block the login.
The block causes the earlier failures.
Time is irrelevant to the rule.
Blocking must wait for a fourth failure.

questions.explanationText: Both the count and time-window conditions are met, so the block follows.

questions.questionText: A factory can meet today's target if both production lines operate for the full shift. One line stops halfway. What can be concluded about the stated sufficient route?

options.text: The target caused the line to stop.
The target is certainly met.
That sufficient route is no longer available; another route would be needed to meet the target.
One line is always sufficient.

questions.explanationText: The specified sufficient combination did not occur. This does not prove impossibility by every route, but it removes the stated one.

questions.questionText: The elevator moves only when all doors are closed. All doors are closed. Does this alone prove the elevator will move?

options.text: Door state is unrelated to movement.
Movement closes every door retroactively.
No. Closed doors are necessary but may not be sufficient without a command and power.
Yes. The elevator must move immediately.

questions.explanationText: 'Only when' gives a necessary safety condition; other causes are still needed for movement.

questions.questionText: A customer receives a refund if the return is within 30 days and the item is unused. Both facts are verified. Under the stated policy, what follows?

options.text: The verified conditions are sufficient for the refund.
The return must be refused.
Only one condition was needed.
The refund causes the item to become unused.

questions.explanationText: Both policy conditions are satisfied, so the specified effect follows.

questions.questionText: A database failover occurs if the primary server is unreachable for five consecutive checks. It fails four checks and responds on the fifth. What follows?

options.text: Failover caused the fifth response.
Failover is not triggered because the required consecutive count was not reached.
The check count cannot affect failover.
Four failures are sufficient.

questions.explanationText: Five consecutive failures are required; the successful fifth check breaks the sequence.

questions.questionText: An applicant is shortlisted only if the coding cutoff is met. Neha misses the cutoff. What can be concluded?

options.text: She cannot be shortlisted under the stated rule.
She must be shortlisted for another reason.
Shortlisting caused her score.
Missing the cutoff is sufficient for selection.

questions.explanationText: The cutoff is necessary. Its absence rules out shortlisting under this rule.

questions.questionText: A plant grows well when it receives suitable light, water, nutrients, and temperature. It receives adequate water alone. Which conclusion is valid?

options.text: Growth causes all water to appear.
Good growth is guaranteed.
Adequate water alone is insufficient to guarantee good growth.
Light and nutrients can never matter.

questions.explanationText: Growth depends on multiple conditions; meeting just one does not establish the outcome.

questions.questionText: A warning email is sent whenever disk usage exceeds 90%. Usage reaches 94%. Is the threshold event sufficient?

options.text: Yes. Exceeding 90% triggers the warning by the stated rule.
The email creates disk usage.
No. Usage must reach exactly 100%.
The threshold and email are independent.

questions.explanationText: The observed value exceeds the trigger threshold, satisfying the stated sufficient condition.

questions.questionText: A tender is considered only if submitted before the deadline. A tender is on time. What may still be true?

options.text: It must be accepted because timeliness is sufficient.
Other requirements cannot exist.
Acceptance caused timely submission.
It may still be rejected for failing other requirements.

questions.explanationText: Timeliness is necessary for consideration, but it does not guarantee acceptance.

questions.questionText: A route is selected automatically when it has the lowest cost and meets the delivery deadline. Route X is cheapest but misses the deadline. What follows?

options.text: The deadline is irrelevant.
Selection makes the route faster.
Lowest cost alone guarantees selection.
Route X is not selected by this rule because one required condition fails.

questions.explanationText: Both low cost and deadline compliance are required; Route X lacks the latter.

questions.questionText: A factory's output fell after both a raw-material shortage and a motor failure. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: Both events are contributing causes of the output decline.
Only one cause can operate at a time.
The output decline caused both earlier events.
The two events are effects of higher output.

questions.explanationText: The scenario explicitly identifies two independent constraints that each contribute to the same fall in output.

questions.questionText: Road construction reduced one lane while a stadium event added thousands of vehicles. Congestion became severe. What caused it?

options.text: Reduced capacity and increased demand jointly contributed.
Congestion caused the event and construction.
Only the stadium could matter.
The events were unrelated to road conditions.

questions.explanationText: The lane closure reduced capacity while the event raised traffic volume; their interaction produced severe congestion.

questions.questionText: Sales declined after a competitor launched a cheaper product and the company increased its own price. Which is correct?

options.text: The two price events guarantee higher sales.
Only advertising can affect sales.
Both competitive pricing events can contribute to the decline.
Lower sales caused both price decisions.

questions.explanationText: A cheaper substitute and a higher own price both provide plausible, stated reasons for customers to switch or buy less.

questions.questionText: A project slipped because requirements arrived late and two engineers were reassigned. What is the causal structure?

options.text: Two contributing causes led to one common effect: delay.
Engineer reassignment is an effect of finishing early.
The events have no project impact.
The delay caused the late requirements.

questions.explanationText: Late inputs and reduced staffing independently constrain progress and contribute to the same schedule delay.

questions.questionText: A data centre overheated after the cooling unit failed while outside temperature was unusually high. Which assessment is strongest?

options.text: Only outside temperature can affect a data centre.
Cooling failure and extreme heat jointly contributed to overheating.
Overheating caused the weather.
Neither condition relates to temperature.

questions.explanationText: One factor removed cooling capacity and the other increased heat load, creating interacting causes.

questions.questionText: Employee turnover rose after workloads increased and a competing firm offered substantially higher salaries. What follows?

options.text: Only workload can influence turnover.
The two conditions are effects of the resignations.
Turnover caused the competitor's offer.
Both conditions are plausible contributing causes supported by the scenario.

questions.explanationText: Higher burden and attractive alternatives can jointly lead employees to leave.

questions.questionText: Crop loss occurred after an irrigation failure during an extended dry spell. Identify the structure.

options.text: Crop loss created the dry spell.
A dry spell and irrigation failure combined to produce water stress and crop loss.
Either event proves the other did not occur.
Neither affects water availability.

questions.explanationText: Natural rainfall was low and backup irrigation failed, so both causes combined to deprive crops of water.

questions.questionText: Website downtime lasted longer because the primary server failed and the backup configuration was incorrect.

options.text: Neither event affects availability.
The backup configuration repaired the server.
The long outage caused the primary failure.
The failure initiated the outage, and the bad backup prolonged it.

questions.explanationText: The primary failure caused initial downtime; the backup defect prevented rapid recovery.

questions.questionText: A delivery arrived late because the truck broke down and the replacement driver encountered a road closure.

options.text: Only the customer's address matters.
The obstacles are effects of delivery completion.
The breakdown and road closure formed successive contributing causes.
Late arrival caused both obstacles.

questions.explanationText: The first event created a delay and the later closure added another, producing the common final effect.

questions.questionText: A bank branch queue grew because one counter closed and customer arrivals peaked at lunchtime.

options.text: The queue closed the counter retroactively.
Lower service capacity and higher arrivals jointly enlarged the queue.
Neither factor changes waiting demand.
Peak arrivals guarantee a shorter queue.

questions.explanationText: Queue size rises when service capacity falls while arrivals increase.

questions.questionText: A severe storm occurred. Flights were delayed, trees fell on roads, and power lines broke. Which relationship is shown?

options.text: All events are independent.
The three effects caused the storm.
Only the flight delay relates to the storm.
One cause produced several distinct effects.

questions.explanationText: The storm is the common cause of transportation, road, and electricity disruptions.

questions.questionText: A supplier stopped shipping a component. Production slowed, delivery promises were missed, and overtime costs rose. What is the best description?

options.text: Overtime caused the supplier to stop.
The outcomes have separate unrelated causes.
Missed deliveries increased component supply.
The supply stop initiated multiple direct and downstream effects.

questions.explanationText: The supply interruption reduced production; that slowdown then affected deliveries and overtime, creating multiple effects.

questions.questionText: A city introduced a clean-bus fleet. Tailpipe emissions on the route fell and engine noise decreased. What is the structure?

options.text: Emissions caused noise to increase.
The improvements are unrelated to bus technology.
Lower noise caused the fleet purchase.
The fleet change is a common cause of both improvements.

questions.explanationText: Cleaner, quieter bus technology can simultaneously reduce local exhaust and engine noise.

questions.questionText: A warehouse sprinkler pipe burst. Stock became wet and the loading area was closed for cleanup. Which is correct?

options.text: Wet stock caused the pipe to burst.
Cleanup caused the earlier water release.
The burst pipe caused more than one operational effect.
The closure is unrelated to water.

questions.explanationText: The water release damaged stock and necessitated closing the area.

questions.questionText: A software release contained a critical authentication bug. Logins failed and support-call volume rose. Which relation is best?

options.text: Login failure and support calls are unrelated.
Support calls created the software bug.
The bug caused login failures, which also generated more support calls.
The release was caused by user complaints.

questions.explanationText: The defect directly caused failed logins and indirectly drove calls from affected users.

questions.questionText: An unexpected freeze damaged water pipes. Households lost supply and repair requests increased. Identify the common cause.

options.text: The freeze caused both physical damage and downstream service requests.
Supply loss caused temperature to fall.
The statements are independent.
Repair requests caused freezing weather.

questions.explanationText: Freezing produced pipe failures, leading both to loss of supply and demand for repairs.

questions.questionText: A firm automated invoice matching. Manual workload fell and average processing time shortened. What is shown?

options.text: One process change produced two related effects.
Workload and time cannot share a cause.
Short processing time caused the automation purchase.
Automation necessarily increased errors.

questions.explanationText: Automation replaced manual steps, reducing both labour required and elapsed processing time.

questions.questionText: A major event ended near a station. Platform crowding rose and taxi demand outside increased. Which is most plausible?

options.text: The event's end is a common cause of both demand surges.
The two observations prove taxis caused train use.
Taxi demand caused the event to end.
Platform crowding caused people to attend the event.

questions.explanationText: Many attendees leaving together can independently increase demand for both rail and taxis.

questions.questionText: Two departments adopted the same new reporting deadline. Both submitted more overtime claims. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: One department's claims caused the other's.
Claims caused the deadline to be adopted.
The tighter common deadline may have caused overtime in both departments.
Simultaneous timing proves no relation.

questions.explanationText: A shared deadline can be the common cause; neither department's overtime causes the other's.

questions.questionText: Two suppliers improved quality inspection. Both later reported fewer returns. Which common effect is present?

options.text: Fewer returns caused earlier inspection changes in both cases.
The suppliers must have caused each other's returns.
Inspection and returns cannot be related.
Improved inspection by each supplier can contribute to fewer returns.

questions.explanationText: Separate but similar causes—stronger inspections—lead toward the same type of effect: fewer defective products returned.

questions.questionText: The company reduced office space and expanded remote work. Which outcome could be a common effect of both decisions?

options.text: Automatic increase in product demand
Lower facility operating costs
Higher cost from occupying more space
A longer manufacturing line

questions.explanationText: Less occupied space and more remote work can both reduce rent, utilities, and other facility costs.

questions.questionText: A retailer improved product descriptions and added size guides. Which shared outcome are both changes intended to cause?

options.text: Slower product discovery in every case
Fewer returns caused by mismatched expectations or size
Higher electricity tariffs
More warehouse damage

questions.explanationText: Better descriptions and sizing information both help customers choose correctly, reducing avoidable returns.

questions.questionText: A plant repaired steam leaks and insulated hot pipes. What common effect can both actions produce?

options.text: A guaranteed rise in raw-material prices
Lower energy loss
Reduced safety from hotter surfaces
More leakage by design

questions.explanationText: Leak repair prevents escaping steam, while insulation reduces heat transfer; both reduce energy waste.

questions.questionText: A company consolidated software licences and removed unused cloud instances. What common effect is intended?

options.text: Automatic growth in headcount
Lower recurring technology costs
Greater payment for unused resources
Longer customer queues

questions.explanationText: Both actions eliminate unnecessary recurring expenditure.

questions.questionText: A college added mock interviews and resume workshops. What common outcome can both initiatives support?

options.text: Reduced server storage
Lower rainfall
Guaranteed employment for every student
Better placement readiness

questions.explanationText: The activities develop complementary job-search skills, though they do not guarantee an offer.

questions.questionText: A municipality repaired leaks and installed water meters. Which common effect may follow?

options.text: Unlimited reservoir capacity
Guaranteed rainfall
Lower avoidable water consumption
Higher leakage from every pipe

questions.explanationText: Repairs stop physical losses, while metering discourages waste; both can reduce avoidable use.

questions.questionText: A call centre improved self-service pages and fixed a recurring billing defect. Which common effect is likely?

options.text: Fewer incoming support calls
More calls caused by the same defect
Longer calls in every case
A larger office building

questions.explanationText: Self-service resolves routine needs and the fix removes one source of complaints, both reducing call demand.

questions.questionText: A manufacturer simplified assembly and standardized components. What common effect can these changes have?

options.text: Guaranteed elimination of all defects
Shorter production time
Higher transport distance
More unique parts by definition

questions.explanationText: Fewer assembly steps and common parts can both reduce handling and production time.

questions.questionText: A bank added fraud alerts and lowered limits for unverified transfers. What common effect do these controls seek?

options.text: Reduced loss from unauthorized transfers
Elimination of legitimate transactions
Higher rainfall
Guaranteed prevention of every crime

questions.explanationText: Alerts speed detection and limits cap exposure, so both aim to reduce fraud losses.

questions.questionText: A company cross-trained staff and documented critical procedures. What shared effect can result?

options.text: Greater continuity when a key employee is absent
Automatic demand growth
More dependence on one person
Guaranteed absence of all employees

questions.explanationText: Cross-training provides substitutes and documentation preserves knowledge; both reduce single-person dependency.

questions.questionText: A store widened aisles and moved displays away from exits. Which common effect can both changes support?

options.text: Safer, less obstructed movement
Higher inventory spoilage
Automatic price reductions
More blocked evacuation routes

questions.explanationText: Both layout changes remove obstacles and improve pedestrian flow, especially during evacuation.

questions.questionText: A logistics firm optimized routes and combined partially filled deliveries. What common effect can follow?

options.text: Higher product manufacturing cost
More distance by necessity
Guaranteed zero delays
Lower fuel use per delivered item

questions.explanationText: Shorter routing and fuller loads both reduce inefficient vehicle travel per item.

questions.questionText: A website compressed images and enabled browser caching. Which common effect is intended?

options.text: Larger transfers on every visit
Faster repeat page loading
Slower local rendering by definition
Guaranteed elimination of server failures

questions.explanationText: Compression reduces payload size and caching avoids repeated downloads, both improving load time.

questions.questionText: A factory introduced guards on moving parts and mandatory lockout procedures. What common effect is sought?

options.text: Faster exposure to moving parts
Elimination of all industrial hazards
Higher product demand
Lower risk of machinery-related injury

questions.explanationText: Physical guards prevent contact and lockout controls unexpected motion; both reduce a specific safety risk.

questions.questionText: A school improved ventilation and staggered lunch periods. Which common effect can both measures support?

options.text: Larger class sizes automatically
Reduced crowding-related exposure to airborne illness
More contaminated drinking water
Guaranteed prevention of every illness

questions.explanationText: Ventilation dilutes airborne particles and staggering reduces close crowding; both lower exposure risk without guaranteeing zero illness.

questions.questionText: Ice-cream sales and sunburn cases both rose in June. What is the best causal interpretation?

options.text: The matching trend proves direct causation.
Buying ice cream directly causes sunburn.
Hot, sunny weather can be a common cause of both increases.
Sunburn forces every person to buy ice cream.

questions.explanationText: Warm sunny conditions encourage ice-cream purchases and outdoor exposure; correlation does not establish that one outcome causes the other.

questions.questionText: Employees who attend optional training often receive higher ratings. What can be concluded from this observation alone?

options.text: No third factor could exist.
Higher ratings occur before and cause all training.
Training certainly raises every attendee's rating.
The association does not prove training caused the ratings; motivation may influence both.

questions.explanationText: Self-selection, prior ability, or motivation may affect both attendance and performance, so causation is not established.

questions.questionText: Neighbourhoods with more fire engines at incidents often report more damage. Which explanation avoids the correlation trap?

options.text: Damage sends engines back in time.
The observations prove engines are ineffective.
Fire engines cause the extra damage.
Larger fires can cause both more damage and deployment of more engines.

questions.explanationText: Incident severity is a common cause of response scale and damage.

questions.questionText: A company observed that teams using a new tool completed projects faster, but the tool was first given to its most experienced teams. What is justified?

options.text: Experience cannot affect project speed.
Experience is a confounding factor, so the tool's causal effect is not isolated.
The tool alone certainly caused all speed gains.
Fast completion created the tool.

questions.explanationText: Because tool assignment was not comparable, team experience could explain some or all of the observed difference.

questions.questionText: Cities with more bicycles also have more cycling injuries. What does the comparison alone support?

options.text: Injuries manufacture bicycles.
More cycling exposure may raise both bicycle counts and the number of injuries; safety per trip is unknown.
The counts have no possible common factor.
Bicycles are proved to make each trip more dangerous.

questions.explanationText: A larger cycling population creates more exposure. Raw totals do not establish greater individual risk or a direct harmful effect.

questions.questionText: A student's marks rose after changing pens before the exam. Which assessment is sound?

options.text: The higher marks caused the earlier purchase.
The timing alone does not establish that the pen caused the higher marks.
No other factor, such as preparation, could matter.
The new pen certainly caused the result.

questions.explanationText: An event occurring before an outcome is not enough to prove causation; preparation and exam difficulty may explain the change.

questions.questionText: Website traffic rose on the same day that office furniture was replaced. What follows?

options.text: Any simultaneous events must share a cause.
Traffic caused the earlier furniture delivery.
New chairs necessarily attract online visitors.
Coincidence in time does not establish that the furniture caused traffic.

questions.explanationText: No plausible mechanism or supporting evidence connects the furniture replacement with website visits.

questions.questionText: Areas with more hospitals report more patients. Which is the best explanation?

options.text: Hospitals create illness in residents.
The correlation proves treatment is harmful.
Larger populations or regional referral demand may cause both more hospitals and more patients.
Patient counts cannot affect planning.

questions.explanationText: Population size and service concentration are plausible common causes; simple counts do not prove hospitals cause illness.

questions.questionText: A retailer's sales and social-media mentions rose after a celebrity event, but the retailer also began a major discount that day. What can be concluded?

options.text: The discount cannot affect purchases.
Sales growth caused both earlier actions.
The celebrity event alone caused all sales growth.
The separate effects of the event and discount cannot be identified from this observation alone.

questions.explanationText: Two plausible causes changed together, so the observation does not isolate either one's contribution.

questions.questionText: Users who enable reminders miss fewer appointments, but highly organized users are more likely to enable reminders. Identify the issue.

options.text: User traits can never affect outcomes.
Organization may cause both reminder use and lower absence, confounding the relationship.
Missed appointments create reminders retroactively.
Reminders are proved to be the sole cause.

questions.explanationText: A pre-existing trait can explain both variables, so the association alone is not proof of causation.

questions.questionText: A factory installed a dashboard, and defects fell the following month; it also replaced a worn machine that month. What is the valid inference?

options.text: The data do not isolate which change caused the decline.
The dashboard alone certainly caused it.
The decline caused both earlier changes.
Machine condition cannot affect defects.

questions.explanationText: Because two relevant interventions occurred together, either or both may have contributed.

questions.questionText: Coffee consumption and overtime hours rose together during a project deadline. Which relation is most plausible?

options.text: The correlation has proved a single direction.
Coffee necessarily creates every overtime hour.
Deadline pressure can be a common cause of both longer work and more coffee consumption.
Overtime cannot influence beverage use.

questions.explanationText: The deadline can independently drive work hours and coffee use, so neither observed variable need directly cause the other.

questions.questionText: A town installed streetlights, after which reported night-time incidents increased. It also introduced easier online reporting. What should be concluded?

options.text: Streetlights certainly increased actual incidents.
Incidents caused lights to be installed after the fact in every case.
Higher reports may reflect easier reporting; the effect of lighting is not established.
Reporting systems cannot change reported counts.

questions.explanationText: A change in measurement or reporting can raise recorded incidents without an increase in actual incidents.

questions.questionText: An app update preceded a battery-drain complaint, but the user's battery health also dropped sharply. Which statement is strongest?

options.text: The update is proven to be the only cause.
Battery health cannot affect drain.
Both the update and degraded battery are plausible causes; more evidence is needed.
The complaint caused the battery to age.

questions.explanationText: Two plausible causal factors are present, so exclusive attribution is unsupported.

questions.questionText: Absence rates fell after a wellness poster campaign, while the seasonal flu wave ended in the same week. What is correct?

options.text: Fewer absences caused the earlier posters.
The end of the flu wave is a competing explanation, so the poster's effect is not isolated.
Flu levels cannot affect absence.
The poster alone certainly caused the fall.

questions.explanationText: The common timing of another relevant change prevents a confident single-cause claim.

questions.questionText: A school with tablets achieved high scores, but it admitted students through a highly selective exam. What is the causal caution?

options.text: Selection cannot affect academic performance.
Scores caused the school to buy tablets before admission.
Student selection may explain the scores, so tablet impact is not established by comparison alone.
Tablets necessarily caused all high scores.

questions.explanationText: The groups differ in prior selection, a confounder that can affect outcomes.

questions.questionText: A road was widened, and congestion worsened a year later while the nearby population grew rapidly. What is supported?

options.text: Widening certainly caused all congestion.
Congestion caused the earlier construction.
Population growth is a competing cause; worsening congestion does not prove widening caused it.
Population cannot affect traffic.

questions.explanationText: Traffic demand changed substantially, so before-after timing alone cannot identify the road change's effect.

questions.questionText: A manager arrived before a network outage. Which conclusion is valid?

options.text: Earlier arrival proves causation.
Arrival before the outage does not by itself show the manager caused it.
All preceding events cause later ones.
The outage caused the manager to arrive in the past.

questions.explanationText: Temporal precedence is necessary for a cause but not sufficient; no mechanism is supplied.

questions.questionText: Online searches for umbrellas rise before reported rainfall because people see forecasts. How should the order be interpreted?

options.text: A forecast can cause searches before the rain; the searches do not cause rainfall.
Searches cause clouds to form.
Later rain must cause earlier searches directly.
The two events cannot share information.

questions.explanationText: Forecast information is an earlier common factor that explains advance purchasing interest.

questions.questionText: Complaints rose before an outage was officially announced. What is the most reasonable explanation?

options.text: Users may have experienced the outage before the announcement; the announcement is not the cause of the complaints.
An announcement must precede every user impact.
Complaints necessarily caused the technical outage.
The timing proves independence.

questions.explanationText: Operational effects can begin before formal communication, so the apparent ordering does not reverse the physical cause.

questions.questionText: A fall in inventory was recorded before the sales report was issued. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: The events must be unrelated.
Inventory records can never precede reports.
Sales may have reduced inventory before the report documented them.
The later report caused the earlier stock movement.

questions.explanationText: A report records earlier transactions; publication time is not the causal time of the sales.

questions.questionText: A company announced layoffs after profits fell. Which is the most defensible direction in this case?

options.text: The announcement caused the earlier recorded decline.
Any layoffs always raise profit immediately.
The events have no possible relation.
The profit decline prompted the later layoff decision.

questions.explanationText: The stated ordering and business mechanism support falling profits as a cause of the later decision, not vice versa.

questions.questionText: A safety inspection followed a machine accident. Does the inspection cause the accident?

options.text: Time order is irrelevant to every causal claim.
Both must be effects of machine repair.
Yes, because the inspection is mentioned second.
No. The accident prompted the later inspection.

questions.explanationText: The inspection is a response to the accident, so treating it as the accident's cause reverses the chronology.

questions.questionText: A refund was issued before the customer received the notification email. What caused what?

options.text: Receiving email is necessary for an earlier transaction.
Approval of the refund caused both the transaction and the later notification.
The later email caused the earlier refund.
The two events prove no process exists.

questions.explanationText: A backend approval can be the common cause; notification delivery may lag behind the actual refund.

questions.questionText: A server alert appeared after the system had already slowed. Which interpretation fits monitoring delays?

options.text: The underlying fault may cause both slowdown and a later alert.
The alert necessarily caused the earlier slowdown.
Alerts are always unrelated to faults.
Slowdown cannot precede detection.

questions.explanationText: Monitoring detects an existing condition; delayed detection can make the effect visible before the alert.

questions.questionText: A river gauge warning was sent after water had entered a low road. Which is correct?

options.text: The order proves the gauge controls the river.
Flooding caused the rain to begin.
The message caused the earlier water rise.
Rising water caused both flooding and the later warning; the warning did not cause flooding.

questions.explanationText: The physical water rise precedes both its road impact and the warning generated from measurements.

questions.questionText: A customer review was posted after a product failed. What is the causal direction?

options.text: Both are necessarily independent.
The failure prompted the review.
The review caused the earlier failure.
Posting a review repairs the product.

questions.explanationText: The review is a response to the product experience, not its preceding cause.

questions.questionText: A recall notice appeared after some devices overheated. What is the best relation?

options.text: The notice caused earlier overheating.
The notice is a sufficient cause of hardware heat.
Overheating reports led to the recall notice.
The events cannot be connected.

questions.explanationText: Safety incidents and reports can prompt a later recall; the notice does not create past defects.

questions.questionText: A drop in website conversions followed a page redesign, but a payment outage occurred throughout the same period. What is the correct judgment?

options.text: Lower conversions caused both prior events.
A payment outage cannot affect purchases.
The outage is a competing cause, so the redesign's effect cannot be isolated.
The redesign alone is proved causal.

questions.explanationText: Two simultaneous, relevant changes prevent unique attribution.

questions.questionText: Customers using premium support renew more often, but premium support is offered mainly to large long-term customers. What is the issue?

options.text: Account characteristics cannot matter.
Premium support is proved to cause every renewal.
Customer size and tenure may confound the observed association.
Renewal causes earlier support assignment in all cases.

questions.explanationText: The groups differ systematically before support, so higher renewal may reflect those differences.

questions.questionText: A city with many parks reports more outdoor exercise. Which conclusion is cautious?

options.text: Parks are proved to be the sole cause.
Parks may encourage exercise, but resident preferences or planning choices could also cause both.
Exercise creates all parks immediately.
No causal investigation is possible.

questions.explanationText: The association is plausible but does not eliminate selection and common-cause explanations.

questions.questionText: Branches with more staff process more transactions, but staffing is assigned according to customer demand. What does this imply?

options.text: Transactions cannot influence staffing plans.
Demand may cause both higher staffing and more transactions.
Extra staff alone is proved to create demand.
The association proves staff are unnecessary.

questions.explanationText: Management allocates staff where demand is already high, creating a common-cause explanation.

questions.questionText: Teams with fewer defects hold more review meetings, but teams schedule extra reviews after past quality problems. What is the causal difficulty?

options.text: Meeting frequency may respond to prior defects, so simple correlation can mask direction and timing.
The observation proves no relationship.
Meetings certainly eliminate every defect.
Defects can never influence review policy.

questions.explanationText: Review frequency is not randomly assigned and may itself be an effect of earlier quality outcomes.

questions.questionText: Households with solar panels use more electricity on average, but they also tend to own larger homes. What is a valid conclusion?

options.text: Home size may be a common cause; the figures do not show panels increase consumption.
Solar panels certainly cause higher demand.
Electricity use installs panels automatically.
Home size cannot affect electricity use.

questions.explanationText: Larger homes may both consume more energy and be more likely to install panels.

questions.questionText: Stores playing music showed longer visits, but only flagship stores used music. Which factor complicates causation?

options.text: Visit length caused music to exist.
Music is proved to cause all longer visits.
Store type cannot influence customers.
Flagship-store size and attractions may affect visit duration as well as music use.

questions.explanationText: The treatment is mixed with store type, so the causal effect of music is not isolated.

questions.questionText: A recruitment campaign and a salary increase began together, followed by more applications. What can be inferred?

options.text: Applications caused both earlier decisions.
The campaign alone is certainly responsible.
Salary cannot affect applications.
Either or both changes may have caused the increase; their separate effects are unknown.

questions.explanationText: Simultaneous plausible causes make a single-cause conclusion unjustified.

questions.questionText: A hospital's waiting time fell after a new scheduler was installed, while a nearby clinic reopened and diverted patients. What is correct?

options.text: Waiting time caused the clinic to reopen.
Patient demand cannot affect waiting time.
The scheduler alone is proved causal.
Lower demand from the reopened clinic is a competing explanation.

questions.explanationText: Both scheduling efficiency and reduced arrivals can lower waiting, so attribution requires more evidence.

questions.questionText: A company with flexible hours has lower turnover, but it introduced flexible hours mainly in high-performing units. What is the caution?

options.text: Flexible hours guarantee retention.
Turnover cannot influence policy choices.
Differences between units may explain turnover; causal impact is not established.
Unit performance is irrelevant.

questions.explanationText: Non-comparable groups create confounding, so association does not prove the policy's effect.

questions.questionText: Air pollution and public-transport use both rose during a festival week. Which inference is sound?

options.text: Pollution caused the festival to occur.
The events cannot share a cause.
Buses caused all pollution.
Festival travel can increase both; public transport use alone is not proved to cause pollution.

questions.explanationText: The festival is a plausible common driver of travel demand and emissions from multiple sources.

questions.questionText: A rise in bottled-water sales coincided with more reports of discoloured tap water. What is the likely causal structure?

options.text: A water-quality problem may cause both reports and bottled-water purchases.
Coincidence proves no relationship is possible.
Reports are caused only by sales figures.
Buying bottled water discolours tap water.

questions.explanationText: The underlying tap-water issue explains both the observations without one directly causing the other.

questions.questionText: A retailer cut prices, increased advertising, and expanded store hours in the same week; sales rose. Which conclusion is strongest?

options.text: Price alone certainly caused the entire rise.
Advertising cannot affect sales.
The combined intervention may have caused the rise, but the effect of each component is not separately established.
Higher sales caused all three earlier decisions.

questions.explanationText: Multiple plausible causes changed together. The bundle may explain the outcome, but observational timing cannot allocate causal contribution.

questions.questionText: A primary database failed. The standby database was healthy, but failover did not occur because the network link between sites was down. What directly prevented recovery?

options.text: The failed inter-site network link
The healthy standby database
The users who attempted login
The later incident report

questions.explanationText: The original database failure caused the outage, but the unavailable network path directly prevented the standby from taking over.

questions.questionText: A factory requires both compressed air and electrical power for a line. A storm cut power while an unrelated leak reduced air pressure. The line stopped. Which is correct?

options.text: The stoppage caused the storm and leak.
Because two causes exist, neither is relevant.
Air pressure is sufficient even without power.
Either missing requirement could stop the line; both failures contributed to the observed stoppage.

questions.explanationText: Both are necessary operating inputs. Losing either is enough to stop production, and both were absent here.

questions.questionText: A company saw fewer support calls after fixing a bug and removing the phone number from its website. What can be concluded?

options.text: Removing the number cannot affect call volume.
Fewer calls prove customer problems increased.
The call decline cannot by itself distinguish genuine issue reduction from reduced access to phone support.
The bug fix alone certainly explains every missing call.

questions.explanationText: One change may reduce problems while the other changes the measurement channel; call count alone does not isolate service quality.

questions.questionText: A reservoir falls during a drought. Restrictions reduce consumption, yet the level continues to decline more slowly. Which causal statement fits?

options.text: Restrictions caused the drought.
Continued decline proves restrictions had no effect.
Consumption and reservoir level are unrelated.
Drought remains a cause of decline, while restrictions counteract part of its effect.

questions.explanationText: Multiple forces act simultaneously: low inflow lowers storage, while reduced use slows—but need not reverse—the decline.

questions.questionText: A security team blocks an attacking address, after which attack traffic falls but legitimate errors rise because customers shared that address. Which analysis is correct?

options.text: One action produced a desired effect and an unintended side effect.
The errors caused the earlier attack.
Blocking cannot have multiple effects.
Falling attack traffic proves no customers were affected.

questions.explanationText: The block reduced malicious traffic from the address while also denying legitimate users behind it.

questions.questionText: A scholarship reminder increased completed applications but not total registrations. What is the most direct supported effect?

options.text: It reduced every applicant's eligibility.
It helped some already registered applicants finish submission.
It caused more people to register.
Completion caused the earlier reminder.

questions.explanationText: With registrations unchanged and completions higher, the supported mechanism is improved follow-through among existing registrants.

questions.questionText: A firm added servers, but response time did not improve because a single database remained saturated. Which statement is best?

options.text: Response time caused the earlier purchase.
Adding servers caused database saturation in every case.
No infrastructure change can improve response time.
Server capacity was not sufficient; the database bottleneck limited the effect.

questions.explanationText: End-to-end performance is constrained by the remaining bottleneck, so one capacity increase need not be sufficient.

questions.questionText: A training programme is offered only to volunteers. Participants later outperform nonparticipants. What evidence would best strengthen a causal claim?

options.text: Comparable volunteers randomly assigned to receive training now or later
A testimonial from the highest scorer
Proof that training occurred before the test only
A larger difference in group size

questions.explanationText: Random assignment among comparable volunteers reduces self-selection and makes training the key systematic difference.

questions.questionText: A town wants to know whether a new bus lane reduced travel time. Which comparison best supports causation?

options.text: Passengers' guesses about speed
Travel time only on one unusually quiet day after opening
Changes on the affected route compared with similar routes without the lane over the same period
The colour of buses before and after

questions.explanationText: A contemporaneous comparison helps separate the lane's effect from weather, demand, and citywide trends.

questions.questionText: Two alarms activate after a pressure spike: one shuts a valve and the other notifies staff. How are the alarm outcomes related?

options.text: The notification causes the shutdown alarm.
The valve action caused the earlier spike.
Only one alarm can have a cause.
They are parallel effects of the same pressure event, not causes of each other.

questions.explanationText: The common sensor condition triggers separate response paths.

questions.questionText: A delayed shipment causes a factory to use safety stock, preventing production loss. What is the role of safety stock?

options.text: It interrupts the causal chain between shipment delay and production loss.
It causes the supplier's earlier delay.
It is an effect of production loss only.
It guarantees shipments are never late.

questions.explanationText: The delay would normally create a shortage, but the buffer supplies components and blocks that downstream effect.

questions.questionText: A price increase lowers unit demand, but total revenue rises. Which statement is logically consistent?

options.text: Revenue cannot rise when demand falls.
The observations must have independent causes.
Lower quantity makes price rise retroactively.
The higher price per unit more than offsets the fall in quantity sold.

questions.explanationText: Revenue equals price times quantity. A sufficient percentage price rise can outweigh a smaller percentage fall in units.

questions.questionText: A company deploys a patch after failures begin; failures then decline. Which fact most weakens the claim that the patch caused the decline?

options.text: Similar patched systems also improved.
The patch targeted the failing component.
Traffic simultaneously returned from an abnormal peak to normal levels.
The patch was installed before the decline.

questions.explanationText: A simultaneous traffic reduction is an alternative cause that could explain the decline independently of the patch.

questions.questionText: A new filter lowers particulate emissions, but measured neighbourhood pollution remains unchanged because wildfire smoke increases. What follows?

options.text: The unchanged total does not prove the filter had no effect; another source offset it.
A filter can work only if total pollution falls.
Wildfire smoke is an effect of factory emissions.
The filter caused the wildfire.

questions.explanationText: Observed pollution is the sum of sources. Improvement in one source can be masked by worsening elsewhere.

questions.questionText: An office mandates stronger passwords. Account takeovers fall, while password-reset requests rise. Which interpretation is valid?

options.text: A cause cannot produce effects in opposite directions.
The policy plausibly produced both a security benefit and an usability cost.
Reset requests caused the earlier mandate.
Lower takeovers prove resets did not rise.

questions.explanationText: Stronger passwords can be harder to guess yet easier for users to forget, yielding two different effects.

questions.questionText: A bridge closure shifts traffic to a bypass. Travel time on the original route is no longer measurable, while bypass congestion rises. What is the direct effect?

options.text: Closure guarantees lower travel time everywhere.
Bypass congestion caused the earlier closure.
The routes are causally independent.
Traffic diversion increases demand on the bypass.

questions.explanationText: Closing the bridge forces vehicles onto alternatives, directly raising bypass traffic and potentially congestion.

questions.questionText: A company reduces defects by slowing the line, but output also falls. Which causal pattern is shown?

options.text: Output and quality cannot share a cause.
Fewer defects cause the line to have slowed earlier.
One operational change causes a quality improvement and a productivity trade-off.
Slower speed guarantees higher output.

questions.explanationText: Reduced speed allows more controlled processing but lowers throughput, producing two effects from one change.

questions.questionText: A warning system sends alerts only after three sensors agree. One faulty sensor reports danger, while two report normal. Why is no alert sent?

options.text: One sensor is always sufficient.
The necessary agreement threshold is not met.
No alert caused the sensor to fail.
Normal readings prove danger is impossible.

questions.explanationText: The logic requires three agreeing sensors; a single report cannot satisfy that condition.

questions.questionText: After a road toll increased, traffic fell on the tolled road and rose on a free parallel road. What is the best causal account?

options.text: Traffic on the free road caused the earlier toll decision.
The toll increase encouraged some drivers to substitute the free route, producing both effects.
The two traffic changes must be unrelated.
A higher toll forces total travel to increase.

questions.explanationText: Route substitution is a common mechanism linking the price change to opposite traffic movements on the two roads.
